lesson.title: Working the Z-Score Formula in Both Directions
lesson.summary: Calculating z-scores means applying the formula z equals x minus mean divided by standard deviation in either direction, converting a raw value into a z-score or converting a target z-score back into a raw value.
lesson.body:
Once you understand what a z-score means, calculating one is a matter of careful substitution into a short formula: z equals x minus mean, divided by standard deviation. The two ingredients you always need are the mean and the standard deviation of the distribution the value belongs to; without both of those, a raw value cannot be converted into a z-score at all, since the z-score describes a value's position relative to that specific mean and spread.

Suppose a set of standardized test scores has a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100, and a particular student scores 650. To calculate this student's z-score, first find the deviation: 650 minus 500 equals 150. Then divide by the standard deviation: 150 divided by 100 equals 1.5. This student's z-score is 1.5, meaning the score of 650 sits exactly one and a half standard deviations above the mean of 500.

The formula also works in reverse, which is just as important a skill. If you are told a target z-score and need to find the corresponding raw value, rearrange the formula to x equals mean plus z times standard deviation. Using the same test with mean 500 and standard deviation 100, what raw score corresponds to a z-score of negative 2? Multiply z by the standard deviation: negative 2 times 100 equals negative 200. Add this to the mean: 500 plus negative 200 equals 300. So a z-score of negative 2 on this test corresponds to a raw score of 300, two full standard deviations below the mean.

A common error is mixing up the order of subtraction or forgetting which direction the formula runs. Always subtract the mean from the raw value, not the other way around, since reversing the subtraction flips the sign of every z-score and turns above average values negative. It also helps to sanity check your answer: if the raw value is above the mean, the z-score must come out positive; if the raw value is below the mean, the z-score must come out negative. In the worked examples above, 650 is above the mean of 500, and the z-score of 1.5 is correctly positive, while 300 is below the mean of 500, matching its negative z-score of negative 2.

A second useful check is unit consistency: the mean, the standard deviation, and the raw value must all be measured on the same scale before you subtract or multiply. If a problem gives you a mean in one unit and a raw score in another, converting everything to matching units first is a required step, not an optional one, because the formula has no way to detect a unit mismatch on its own; it will produce a number regardless, and that number will simply be wrong.

These two directions, raw value to z-score and z-score back to raw value, cover essentially every computational z-score question you will encounter. The harder, more interesting work is interpreting what a calculated z-score actually tells you about a value's position in its distribution, which is exactly where the next section picks up.
